group.title: Emotions
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: Extremely angry.
examples: She was {furious} when someone broke her new phone.
wrong: He was furious, so he thanked them and smiled.

words.meaning: Finding something funny.
examples: The children were {amused} by the clown’s silly tricks.
wrong: He was amused by the joke, so he never laughed or smiled.

words.meaning: Very unhappy.
examples: I felt {miserable} when I had the flu.
wrong: She felt miserable, so she smiled and danced all day.

words.meaning: Very happy and pleased.
examples: We were {delighted} to hear your good news.
wrong: He was delighted by the news and shouted in anger.

words.meaning: Not nice; making you feel bad.
examples: The smell in the bus was very {unpleasant}.
wrong: The beautiful, unpleasant day made everyone smile.

words.meaning: Feeling glad that someone helped you or that something good happened.
examples: I am {thankful} for my family.
wrong: She was thankful for the help, so she was angry with them.

words.meaning: Not able to understand something clearly.
examples: I was {confused} by the long instructions.
wrong: He was confused because everything was perfectly clear.

words.meaning: A good feeling about something you or someone close to you has done.
examples: She smiled with {pride} when her son won.
wrong: He felt pride because he had done something terrible.

words.meaning: The feeling you have when nothing interests you.
examples: I started drawing on my notes out of {boredom}.
wrong: The film was so exciting that I yawned with boredom.

words.meaning: The feeling of being shy or silly in front of other people.
examples: His face went red with {embarrassment}.
wrong: She felt embarrassment because everyone praised her quietly in private.

words.meaning: The sad feeling when something is not as good as you hoped.
examples: To our {disappointment}, the concert was canceled.
wrong: It was a disappointment, much better than we ever hoped.

words.meaning: A feeling of great pleasure.
examples: The kids shouted with {delight} when they saw the puppy.
wrong: To her delight, she failed every test.

words.meaning: Very surprised and upset by something bad you did not expect.
examples: We were {shocked} by the news of the accident.
wrong: She was shocked, because she knew it would happen all along.

words.meaning: To feel sad and without energy for a while.
examples: I {feel down} when it rains all week.
wrong: He felt down, so he was full of energy and joy.

words.meaning: A feeling of being very happy and eager about something.
examples: The children could hardly sleep from {excitement}.
wrong: Full of excitement, he yawned and fell asleep, bored.

words.meaning: Feeling happy and friendly.
examples: Dad is {in a good mood} today, so let’s ask him.
wrong: She was in a good mood, so she shouted at everyone.

words.meaning: Feeling angry or unhappy for a while.
examples: Don’t talk to him; he’s {in a bad mood}.
wrong: He was in a bad mood, smiling and joking with everyone.

words.meaning: Making you feel sad or worried.
examples: The news about the fire was very {upsetting}.
wrong: The upsetting news made everyone cheerful.

words.meaning: Making you feel afraid.
examples: The storm was {frightening}, with loud thunder all night.
wrong: The frightening story made us feel safe and calm.

words.meaning: To breathe out slowly and loudly because you are tired, sad or relieved.
examples: He {sighed} and sat down after the long day.
wrong: She sighed by breathing in fast and holding her breath.

words.meaning: When your face goes red because you feel shy or embarrassed.
examples: She {blushed} when he said she was pretty.
wrong: He blushed, and his face went completely white.

words.meaning: Very anxious about something, so you cannot stop thinking about it.
examples: Mom was {worried sick} when I came home late.
wrong: She was worried sick, so she felt calm and slept well.

words.meaning: To shake a little because you are afraid, nervous or cold.
examples: Her hands {trembled} before the big speech.
wrong: He trembled with fear while his body stayed perfectly still.

words.meaning: Feeling that something good will happen.
examples: We are {hopeful} that she will get better soon.
wrong: He felt hopeful because he was sure everything would go wrong.

words.meaning: Pleased because you got what you wanted.
examples: Are you {satisfied} with your new phone?
wrong: She was satisfied with the meal, so she complained to the cook.

words.meaning: Having or showing strong feelings.
examples: She got very {emotional} at her daughter’s wedding.
wrong: He was very emotional and showed no feelings at all.

words.meaning: Calm and quiet, without worry.
examples: I feel {peaceful} when I sit by the lake.
wrong: The peaceful crowd shouted and fought all night.

words.meaning: To make someone feel less sad or worried.
examples: She {comforted} her friend after the bad news.
wrong: He comforted the crying child by shouting at her.

words.meaning: Making you feel shy, silly or ashamed in front of others.
examples: Falling over on stage was so {embarrassing}.
wrong: It was embarrassing, so I felt proud and relaxed.

words.meaning: Not as good as you hoped.
examples: The ending of the book was {disappointing}.
wrong: The meal was disappointing; it was even better than we hoped.

words.meaning: Making you a little angry.
examples: The noise from next door is really {annoying}.
wrong: The music was annoying, so it made me feel calm and happy.

words.meaning: Making you feel calm and rested.
examples: A hot bath is very {relaxing}.
wrong: The relaxing film made my heart race with fear.

words.meaning: Feeling worried or embarrassed, not at ease.
examples: I felt {uncomfortable} when they started to argue.
wrong: She felt uncomfortable, completely calm and at ease.

words.meaning: In a happy way.
examples: The children played {happily} in the garden.
wrong: She smiled happily, feeling sad and angry inside.

words.meaning: Drops of water that come from your eyes when you cry.
examples: {Tears} ran down her face at the sad ending.
wrong: He wiped the tears from his dry eyes.

words.meaning: The happy sound people make when something is funny.
examples: The room was full of {laughter}.
wrong: Their loud laughter showed how sad they were.

words.meaning: To suddenly feel so afraid that you can’t think clearly.
examples: Don’t {panic}; just walk to the exit slowly.
wrong: He panicked and stayed perfectly calm and thoughtful.

words.meaning: To feel sad for someone because they have a problem.
examples: I {feel sorry for} her because she lost her job.
wrong: I felt sorry for him because he won a big prize.

words.meaning: Making you feel worried and under pressure.
examples: Moving house is very {stressful}.
wrong: It was a stressful day, so I felt totally relaxed.

words.meaning: To smile widely.
examples: He {grinned} when he saw his present.
wrong: She grinned with a sad, closed mouth.
